title: On the rock
hookLine: the wise man built his house upon a rock (Matthew 7:24–27)
tomorrow: the result isn't up to you yet. what do you do while you wait?

cards: Rain on a roof, hard enough that people stop talking. Wind leaning on the windows. A gutter overflowing somewhere.

That's the sound of the last story in the sermon, and yesterday's question has an answer: a house on rock in a storm sounds exactly as loud as the house next door. Two houses. One storm, the same for both.
The difference isn't in the noise.

teach.b: "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock."
Then the other builder, who hears the same sayings and doesn't do them, builds on sand. Same rain, same floods, same wind, "and great was the fall of it." Listen to what's the same.
Both men heard. Same sermon, same words, same weather.
The storm hits both houses. Doing the sayings, in this story, isn't a promise of no storms. The whole difference is one word: doeth.
Not how much each man knew, not how well he understood, but whether he did it. And Matthew says when Jesus finished, "the people were astonished at his doctrine."
That's the teaching Christians take from it: the sermon is meant to be lived, not admired.
The letter of James says it plainly: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only."
One to tell a friend: rock comes back later in Matthew, when Jesus says to Peter, "upon this rock I will build my church."

how: Christians read the two builders (Matthew 7:24–27) as the Sermon on the Mount's closing call to live what it teaches; some children learn it as a song, and it is paired with James 1:22, be doers of the word.

o: the stone tablets Moses carried down the mountain
a life built on what you do, not only on what you hear
a church built high on a hill so it can't be flooded

games.q: two builders, one storm: tap the pairs.

s: in the story, only the foolish man's house is hit by the storm
the rain, floods and wind beat on both houses; one fell not.
both builders heard the same sayings
the difference is that one did them.
the Sermon on the Mount ends with a prayer
it ends with a story about two houses, and astonished listeners.

games.q: your friend finished a whole course on patience and is still yelling at traffic. what would the house on the rock say?
o: knowing it isn't enough; the rock is doing it, one small practice at a time.
the course failed him; real patience has to come naturally or not at all.
he should take the same course again until the ideas finally sink in.
games.why: both builders heard the same sayings. the one who did them built on rock.

practice: Sit forward and press both feet flat into the floor until you feel the ground push back. Lay one hand on something solid, a table or a wall, and let a little of your weight rest there.
Breathe as if the rain were outside and you were the house.

wordCard.voice: On the rock: the house of the one who hears the sayings and does them, still standing after the storm.

carryVoice: The line to keep: on the rock, which means doing, not only hearing. The Sermon on the Mount, read to the end.
